Problem 1: Algorithms
Problem Statement
Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a unique minimum spanning tree
if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied: (1) For every partition of the
vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight connecting the two subsets is
unique. (2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
1.1
Solution
Theorem 1. Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Then G possesses a unique minimum span-
ning tree if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied:
(1) For every partition of the vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight
connecting the two subsets is unique.
(2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
Proof. We prove both directions separately.
(⇒) Uniqueness implies both properties:
Suppose G has a unique minimum spanning tree T.
Proof of Property (1): Suppose for contradiction that there exists a partition (S, V \S) of
the vertex set and two distinct edges e1, e2 both having the same minimum weight w among
all edges crossing this cut.
Since T is a minimum spanning tree, by the fundamental cut property of MSTs, T must
contain at least one minimum-weight edge crossing the cut (S, V \ S).
Without loss of
generality, suppose e1 ∈T.
Since T is a tree, e1 is a bridge in T, meaning that removing e1 disconnects T into exactly
two components. These components must be precisely S and V \ S (as e1 connects these
two sets).
Now consider T ′ = T −{e1} + {e2}. Since e2 also connects S and V \ S, the graph T ′ is
connected and has |V | −1 edges, hence T ′ is a spanning tree.
Furthermore, since w(e1) = w(e2) = w, we have:
w(T ′) = w(T) −w(e1) + w(e2) = w(T)

historical_source_fields.explanation: The target claim is a finitely refutable universally-quantified statement over finite weighted graphs, and a single small graph refutes it. Exhaustive enumeration over the bounded space below found witnesses at the smallest possible size (n = 3), and the witnesses were re-derived by hand: for the triangle with weights w(0-1)=1, w(0-2)=1, w(1-2)=2 the three spanning trees have exact integer weights 2, 3, 3, so the MST is unique, while the cut ({0}, {1,2}) has two crossing edges both of weight 1. Thus "unique MST => property (1)" is false, and the verbatim structural sentence ("the components of T - e1 must be precisely S and V\S") is false on the same object: T - (0-1) splits into {0,2} and {1}, not {0} and {1,2}, and the attempted exchange T - e1 + e2 is not even a spanning tree. The script prints both the claimed quantity and the recomputed quantity side by side ("claim says count = 1 ...; here that count = 2 > 1"). Every decision uses exact integer arithmetic; MST counts come from brute-force enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets tested for connectivity, so no theorem about tie-breaking is assumed anywhere in the checker. Run time: 8s CPU / 1m44s wall on a load-50 two-core node.
historical_source_fields.flaw: In the (⇒) direction, the proof asserts that if e1 is a minimum-weight edge crossing a cut (S, V\S) and e1 ∈ T, then deleting e1 splits T into exactly the two components S and V\S, so that T' = T − {e1} + {e2} (with e2 the other minimum-weight crossing edge) is again a spanning tree of the same weight, yielding a second MST. The components of T − e1 need not equal (S, V\S), and the exchange can fail entirely; a 3-vertex graph has a unique MST while a cut has two tied minimum-weight crossing edges, so the derived contradiction (and hence the claimed implication "unique MST ⇒ property (1)") is false.

historical_source_fields.witness:
Two independent finite witnesses were found by exhaustive search (all arithmetic in Python ints; connectivity by union-find; MST counts by brute-force enumeration of every (n-1)-subset of edges — no shortcut theorem about ties was assumed).

WITNESS 1 — refutes the IMPLICATION "unique MST => every cut has a unique minimum-weight crossing edge" (the (=>) direction the proof claims to establish).
Triangle on V = {0,1,2} with w(0-1) = 1, w(0-2) = 1, w(1-2) = 2.
- All 3 spanning trees and their exact weights: {01,02} = 2, {01,12} = 3, {02,12} = 3.
- Minimum weight = 2, attained by exactly ONE spanning tree, so the MST is UNIQUE (MST count = 1).
- Cut S = {0}, V\S = {1,2}: crossing edges are 0-1 (w=1) and 0-2 (w=1). Minimum crossing weight = 1, attained by 2 edges.
- Claim says: MST count = 1 forces #(minimum-weight crossing edges) = 1 for every cut. Here MST count = 1 but that count = 2 > 1. So the implication is false.
(A degenerate n=3 witness also exists — the path 0-2 (w=1), 1-2 (w=1), a tree, with cut S={0,1}. The triangle above is the non-degenerate, cycle-containing version.)

WITNESS 2 — refutes the VERBATIM SENTENCE "removing e1 disconnects T into exactly two components ... These components must be precisely S and V\S".
Same triangle: T = {0-1, 0-2} is the (unique) MST; cut S = {0}, V\S = {1,2}; e1 = 0-1 is a tied minimum-weight crossing edge and lies in T.
- Components of T - e1 = {0,2} and {1}. The sentence asserts they are {0} and {1,2}. They are not.
- Consequently the exchange step fails: the partner tied edge e2 = 0-2 is already in T, so T - e1 + e2 = {0-2} is not a spanning tree at all, and no second MST is produced.
The script also reports a version where e2 is NOT already in T and the exchange still fails: n=4, edges 0-3, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 all of weight 1, T = {0-3, 1-2, 2-3}, cut S = {0,1}, e1 = 0-3 in T, e2 = 1-3 not in T; components of T - e1 = {0} and {1,2,3}, not {0,1} and {2,3}, and T - e1 + e2 is not a spanning tree.

Root cause: e1 crossing the cut only guarantees that its two endpoints land in different components of T - e1; the components of T - e1 are determined by T's structure, not by S. The correct direction is the converse ("all cut-minima unique => MST unique"); "unique MST => all cut-minima unique" is simply false, with the weighted triangle (1,1,2) as a minimal counterexample.

prog :: Int → Int
    prog 0 = 0
    prog n = let a = n - 1 ; b = prog a
             in
               if   a + 1 <= (b + 1) * (b + 1)
               then b
               else b + 1
current_fields.explanation: The guard in the extracted program is off by one: it tests `a + 1 <= (b + 1) * (b + 1)`, i.e. (substituting a = n-1) `n <= (b+1)^2`, where the specification R(x, y) = [y^2 <= x < (y+1)^2] requires the STRICT test `n < (b+1)^2`. Consequently, whenever the input n equals (b+1)^2 exactly — where b = prog (n-1) is the correct value floor(sqrt(n-1)) = sqrt(n) - 1 for n a perfect square — the program keeps the stale value b instead of incrementing to b+1. The smallest instance is x = 1: prog 1 = 0, and the claim asserts (prog x)^2 <= x < (prog x + 1)^2, i.e. 0 <= 1 < 1; the lower bound holds (0 <= 1) but the upper bound FAILS, since claim says x < 1 while x = 1 >= 1. Note the error does not propagate past a perfect square: at n = k^2 + 1 the guard n <= (b+1)^2 = k^2 is false, so the value increments back to k = floor(sqrt(k^2+1)), which is why the failure set is exactly the nonzero perfect squares rather than a growing drift. This is a genuine refutation of the unbounded universal claim (not an artifact of the search bound), since x = 1 is a concrete non-negative input of the program's domain and both prog 1 and R(1, 0) were recomputed exactly.

current_fields.problem:
Relating a proof to a Haskell program

I am trying to relate the following [integer square root theorem][1] 

$\forall x: \mathbb{N}, \exists y : \mathbb{N}((y^2 \leq x) \land  (x < (y+1)^2))$

and its proof to its role as a specification of the Integer Square Root `isqrt` ($\lfloor \sqrt{x} \rfloor$) function in a Haskell program.

Below is a [inductive proof][2] of the theorem and the related Haskell program. 
The proof was done using natural deduction in the [Fitch system][3], hence there are notational differences between code and proof e.g. no $\leq$ in Fitch. 

For my question the details of the proof are not important. I wish to focus on the base case, and the two cases involving  $\exists$-Elimination and $\lor$-Elimination. 

I used Quickcheck as a reasonable check that the theorem holds in the code. 

I can see that cases **1** and **2** in the proof correspond to the guard conditions in the Haskell definition of `isqrt` function. I did not specify, prove, and implement  the function `isqrt` in any structured way. I just used any examples I could find. I believe that there must some more formal transformation from proof to code that I am missing. So despite having written both the proof and code the precise correspondence between both eludes my comprehension. 

Is there a technical name for this form of proof to program relation?
I would be grateful for an explanation or pointer to the literature.

    module Peano where
    import Test.QuickCheck
    
    data Nat = Z | S Nat deriving Show
    -- addition
    (+@) :: Nat -> Nat -> Nat
    Z +@ y = y
    (S x) +@ y = S (x +@ y)
    -- multiplication
    (*@) :: Nat -> Nat -> Nat
    x *@ Z = Z 
    x *@ S y = (x *@ y) +@ x 
    -- square
    sqr x = x *@ x 
    -- equality
    (=@) :: Nat -> Nat -> Bool
    Z =@ Z  = True
    (S m) =@  (S n) = m =@ n 
    _=@ _  = False 
    
    -- lesst than
    (<@) :: Nat -> Nat -> Bool
    Z <@ Z = False 
    Z <@ x | not(x =@ Z) = True 
    x <@ Z | not(x =@ Z) = False 
    (S x) <@ (S y) = x <@ y 
    
    
    -- less than or equal
    (<=@) :: Nat -> Nat -> Bool
    x <=@ y = if (x =@ y) || (x <@ y) then True else False
    
    
    -- Integer square root function
    isqrt Z = Z
    isqrt (S x) | (sqr (S (isqrt x))) <=@  (S x) = (S (isqrt x))
                | (S x) <@ (sqr (S (isqrt x))) = isqrt x
    
    -- test with Quickcheck
    instance Arbitrary Nat where
     arbitrary = oneof [return Z, (S  <$>  arbitrary) ]
    
    isqrtPostCondition :: Nat  -> Bool
    isqrtPostCondition x  = (sqr (isqrt x) <=@ x) && (x <@ sqr(S (isqrt x)))
    check = quickCheck isqrtPostCondition
    -- +++ OK, passed 100 tests.


  [1]: http://www.nuprl.org/MathLibrary/integer_sqrt/
  [2]: https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2891932/inductive-proof-using-fitch-software
  [3]: https://www.press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/L/bo12734345.html
  [4]: https://i.sstatic.net/Qr4Jp.png

0088 | \section{Introduction}
0089 | A long standing open problem asks whether a binary $[72,36,16]$ Type~II code exists, where Type~II indicates that the code is self-dual and the Hamming weight of all vectors in the code are congruent to $0 \pmod{4}.$  The question has remained open over 40 years and is the first in  a series of open questions about the existence of $[24k,12k,4k+4]$ Type~II codes. A number of attempts have been made to solve this problem, many of which have led to restrictions about the automorphism group of such a code if it exists. We can refer the reader to such works as \cite{Bouyuklieva}, \cite{Boyuklieva-2}, \cite{Nebe}, \cite{OBrien}, \cite{Yankov} and the references therein. The latest works indicate that the automorphism group of a doubly-even $[72,36,16]$ code has order $5$ or divides $24$.

u →v in G.

such that:

Let c(S, T) and c(S′, T ′) denote the capacities of these cuts, which are equal since both
are minimum cuts.
By the definition of a cut, the capacity c(S, T) includes all edges from S to T. Since
u ∈S and v ∈T in (S, T), the edge u →v contributes to c(S, T).
Similarly, in (S′, T ′), since u ∈T ′ and v ∈S′, the edge u →v does not contribute to
c(S′, T ′) (as it goes from T ′ to S′).
Now consider the cut (S ∩S′, T ∪T ′). This is also an (s, t)-cut because:
[U+0088 CONTROL] s ∈S and s ∈S′ (as both are (s, t)-cuts), so s ∈S ∩S′
[U+0088 CONTROL] t ∈T and t ∈T ′, so t ∈T ∪T ′
The capacity of this new cut satisfies:
c(S ∩S′, T ∪T ′) ≤c(S, T) + c(S′, T ′) −c(S ∩T ′, T ∩S′)
However, the edge u →v appears in:
[U+0088 CONTROL] c(S, T) (as u ∈S, v ∈T)
[U+0088 CONTROL] Not in c(S′, T ′) (as u ∈T ′, v ∈S′)
[U+0088 CONTROL] Not in c(S ∩T ′, T ∩S′) (since u ∈S ∩T ′ and v ∈T ∩S′, the edge goes from S ∩T ′ to
T ∩S′)
